Light can cross a vacuum because it is an **electromagnetic wave**, while sound (a mechanical wave) cannot. $4.5 \times 10^{19}$ s comes from multiplying instead of dividing, $2 \times 10^{-3}$ s from dividing the wrong way round, and $50$ s from slipping a power of ten.

prompt: At the top of the atmosphere, the **solar constant** is about $1400\ \text{W m}^{-2}$. On a clear day, the highest insolation (sunlight energy received) at the ground is about $1000\ \text{W m}^{-2}$. Roughly what percentage of the energy is lost on the way down?

hint: Find the loss first, then divide it by the amount you started with.
explanation: Loss $= 1400 - 1000 = 400\ \text{W m}^{-2}$, and $$\dfrac{400}{1400} \times 100 \approx 29\%$$ This energy is **absorbed and scattered** by gases, clouds and dust. 40% divides the loss by 1000 instead of by the starting value, 71% is the fraction that *does* reach the ground, and 0.4% writes the $0.4\ \text{kW}$ loss as if it were a percentage. The solar constant ($1.4\ \text{kW m}^{-2}$) is the energy per second per square metre facing the Sun before any absorption.

image.alt: Sunlight falling on a solar panel in a desert, with a clock beside it

hint: Energy = intensity × area × time, with intensity in W m⁻² and time in seconds.

Estimates like this show why even a fraction of the Thar desert covered with panels could supply India's electricity.

explanation: Much of the incoming sunlight passes through the air and is **absorbed by the surface**. The warm surface then **re-radiates infrared**, and greenhouse gases absorb part of it, keeping heat near the ground. That is why the troposphere is heated from the Earth's surface. CO₂ mainly traps *outgoing* infrared rather than incoming light, dust absorbs only a little sunlight, and reflected light leaves rather than heats.

explanation: **Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour** absorb the infrared re-radiated by the surface, preventing it from escaping into space. Nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%) make up most of the air but do not trap this heat, and argon is present only in small amounts. Without greenhouse gases the Earth would be too cold for life.

prompt: A $2\ \text{m}^2$ patch of snow with an **albedo of 0.8** receives sunlight of $1000\ \text{W m}^{-2}$. How much power does the snow **absorb**?

image.alt: Equal sunlight falling on four different surfaces

hint: Albedo is the fraction reflected. What fraction is left over?
explanation: Power falling on the patch $= 1000 \times 2 = 2000\ \text{W}$. **Albedo** is the fraction reflected, so $0.8 \times 2000 = 1600\ \text{W}$ bounces off and $$P_{\text{absorbed}} = (1 - 0.8) \times 2000 = 400\ \text{W}$$ 1600 W is the *reflected* part, 200 W forgets the area, and 800 W is the reflected power for only $1\ \text{m}^2$. High-albedo snow stays cool because it absorbs so little.

Trees in cities give out extra heat through transpiration

explanation: Built-up materials such as **concrete, brick, steel and asphalt** absorb solar radiation, retain heat and **re-radiate** it, warming the city. A few metres of building height makes no difference to the Sun's distance, and transpiration cools rather than heats.

prompt: Two equal beams of sunlight strike the Earth, one near the equator and one near a pole. Why do regions near the equator stay **warmer**?

image.alt: Two equal beams of sunlight striking a round Earth at different places

options.text: The equator is much closer to the Sun than the poles
There is no atmosphere above the poles
The equator receives sunlight for all 24 hours of every day
The same energy is concentrated on a smaller area at the equator but spread over a larger area near the poles

hint: Compare the length of the two bright patches made by the beams.
explanation: Because the Earth is a **sphere**, the Sun's rays strike different latitudes at different angles. Near the equator a beam lands almost straight on and its energy is **concentrated** over a small area, while near the poles the same beam is **spread** over a larger area, so each square metre gets less. This uneven heating drives global winds and ocean currents. The difference in distance from the Sun is negligible.

The centre of the disc would receive no sunlight at all
Nothing would change, because heating depends only on distance from the Sun

hint: Look at the angle at which the rays meet the disc compared with the ball.
explanation: On a sphere the rays meet the surface at different angles, so energy per square metre falls from the equator to the poles. A flat disc facing the Sun would meet every ray **at the same angle**, so insolation would be **nearly the same everywhere**. Without this temperature difference, the pressure belts and planetary winds that it drives would be much weaker. This shows that the Earth's **shape** controls the uneven heating.

explanation: Intense heating makes air rise at the equator (**equatorial low**). High up it moves poleward, cools, becomes denser and **sinks near 30° N and 30° S**, forming the **sub-tropical high pressure belts**. prompt: Planetary winds do not blow straight from high pressure to low pressure. They follow **curved paths**. What causes this?

image.alt: The Earth with lines of latitude and curved surface winds

options.text: Uneven heating of land and sea
The Earth's rotation on its axis, which deflects winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere
The tilt of the Earth's axis, which bends winds towards the summer hemisphere
Friction with ocean currents, which drags the winds sideways

hint: The ground beneath the moving air is itself turning.
explanation: Pressure differences set the air moving, but the **Earth's rotation** deflects it from a straight path: to the **right in the Northern Hemisphere** and to the **left in the Southern Hemisphere**. Uneven heating creates the pressure belts but does not bend the winds, and it is winds that drag ocean water, not the other way round. The same rotation also turns ocean currents into gyres.

explanation: Intense **heating** at the equator makes air **rise**, creating the **equatorial low**. From there it **flows back to the equator** along the surface, completing one circulation cycle. Uneven heating, not the wind itself, powers this loop.

chapter: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life
prompt: What is the main role of **biogeochemical cycles** in an ecosystem?

image.alt: A plant, a person, a campfire and a rusting bucket under the open sky

options.text: To provide food directly to every organism
To create new elements for living things to use
To remove all pollutants and toxins from organisms
To recycle essential nutrients between living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) parts

hint: 'Cycle' means the same atoms are used again and again.
explanation: A **biogeochemical cycle** is the cyclic movement of matter and energy between the **biotic** and **abiotic** parts of the Earth. It keeps nutrients such as carbon, nitrogen and oxygen **recycled** and available to support life, and it helps ecosystems recover from disturbances. Cycles move existing atoms around; they do not make new elements or feed organisms directly.

prompt: Tap the place where water vapour is turning back into tiny droplets, that is, where **condensation** is happening.

image.alt: Water moving between the sea, the sky, a mountain, a tree and the ground, with numbered markers

hint: Condensation is the reverse of evaporation: rising vapour cools and becomes liquid again, before any rain falls.
explanation: Water **evaporates** from the sea, rises, cools and **condenses** into droplets that form clouds. The clouds release **precipitation** (rain, hail or snow) over the hills. The water then runs off in rivers back to the ocean, while some seeps down to become **groundwater**, and plants return vapour to the air by **transpiration**.

prompt: Follow a drop of sea water through the water cycle. Arrange the steps in order.

image.alt: Water moving between the sea, the sky, a mountain, a tree and the ground

items.text: It falls as rain on the hills
The Sun heats the sea and the water evaporates
It reaches the ocean again
The vapour cools and condenses into a cloud
It runs off the slopes into a river

hint: Sunlight is the energy source that starts the cycle.
explanation: Solar energy drives **evaporation**; the vapour rises, cools and **condenses** into clouds; water returns as **precipitation**; it **runs off** into rivers and finally flows back to the **ocean**. Along the way water dissolves minerals from soil and rocks and carries nutrients that support life on land and in the sea.

topic: Climate change and the water cycle
prompt: How is **climate change** affecting the water cycle? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Water moving between the sea, the sky, a mountain, a tree and the ground

options.text: A warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, giving heavier rain in some areas
Droughts become more likely in other areas
Melting glaciers add water to rivers and, in the long run, raise sea levels
Sudden bursts of heavy rain increase infiltration and recharge groundwater
More run-off erodes the soil
Warmer air holds less moisture, so rainfall decreases everywhere

hint: Heavy, sudden rain runs off quickly instead of soaking in.
explanation: A warmer atmosphere **holds more moisture**, so some regions get heavier rain (more intense monsoons) while others face **drought**. **Melting glaciers** feed rivers and eventually raise sea levels, threatening coastal cities such as Mumbai and Chennai. Intense bursts of rain cause more **run-off and soil erosion** and *less* infiltration, so groundwater recharge falls and farming in dry months becomes harder.

prompt: Part of the carbon cycle runs over **millions of years**. Tap the carbon store that belongs to this **slow cycle**.

image.alt: Carbon dioxide moving between the air, a tree, an animal, a factory, the ground and the sea, with numbered markers

hint: Dead plants and animals that were buried long ago.
explanation: In the **slow cycle**, buried dead plants and animals are turned over millions of years into **fossil fuels**: coal, oil and gas. Burning them releases that carbon as CO₂ on a very short time scale. The **fast cycle** (days to years) is photosynthesis, respiration, feeding and decomposition by living things.

prompt: Each numbered arrow moves carbon. Match each arrow with the process it shows.

image.alt: Carbon dioxide moving between the air, a tree, an animal, a factory, the ground and the sea, with four numbered arrows

right.text: Respiration
Decomposition
Exchange of CO₂ with ocean water
Photosynthesis
Combustion of fossil fuels

hint: Only one arrow carries CO₂ out of the air into a living thing on land.
explanation: Arrow 1 takes CO₂ from the air into the tree: **photosynthesis**, which turns it into glucose. Arrow 2 returns CO₂ from the animal: **respiration**. Arrow 3 rises from the chimney: **combustion of fossil fuels**. Arrow 4 is the two-way **exchange with the ocean**, where CO₂ forms carbonate and bicarbonate ions used by phytoplankton and shell-makers. Decomposition was the distractor.

prompt: The graph shows that the CO₂ in the atmosphere rose from about $315\ \text{ppm}$ in 1960 to about $420\ \text{ppm}$ today. By roughly what **percentage** has it increased?

image.alt: Graph of carbon dioxide in the air from 1960 to 2025

hint: Percentage increase = rise ÷ starting value × 100.
explanation: Rise $= 420 - 315 = 105\ \text{ppm}$, so $$\dfrac{105}{315} \times 100 \approx 33\%$$ which the textbook rounds to 'about 35%'. 25% divides by the final value, 105% writes the rise in ppm as a percentage, and 75% is $315 \div 420$. The yearly **sawtooth** wiggles are seasonal dips as Northern Hemisphere plants absorb CO₂ while growing.

prompt: Carbon makes up about **49% of the dry weight** of living things. Roughly how much carbon is stored in a dried log weighing $20\ \text{kg}$?

image.alt: A dried log of wood resting on a weighing scale

options.text: $9.8\ \text{kg}$

hint: 49% means 0.49 of the dry mass.
explanation: $$m_{\text{C}} = 0.49 \times 20\ \text{kg} = 9.8\ \text{kg}$$ $0.98$ kg uses 4.9% instead of 49%, $14.2$ kg uses the 71% figure (the share of the world's carbon held in the **oceans**), and $10.2$ kg is the part that is *not* carbon. Burning or rotting the log returns this carbon to the air as CO₂. The atmosphere holds only about 1% of the world's carbon.

prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the correct option.

image.alt: Carbon dioxide moving between the air, land and the sea

assertion: As the oceans get warmer, they become a better carbon sink.
reason: Ocean water absorbs CO₂ from the atmosphere and forms carbonate and bicarbonate ions.
hint: Does warm water hold more or less dissolved gas?
explanation: The assertion is false and the reason is true. The ocean does absorb CO₂, forming **carbonate and bicarbonate ions** used by phytoplankton and shell-forming organisms. But **warmer water reduces** the ocean's capacity to absorb CO₂, so it becomes a *weaker* sink. Meanwhile, extra CO₂ makes sea water **more acidic**, threatening plankton and coral reefs.

prompt: Tap where **Rhizobium** bacteria live and fix nitrogen from the air for the pea plant.

image.alt: Nitrogen moving between the air, a pea plant and the soil, with numbered markers

hint: Rhizobium lives inside a legume plant, not freely in the soil.
explanation: **Rhizobium** lives in the **root nodules** of legumes such as peas and converts unreactive N₂ into **ammonia** (NH₃). Free-living **Azotobacter** in the soil also fixes nitrogen. **Lightning** fixes a tiny amount as nitrogen oxides, and decomposers such as fungi return ammonia to the soil when organisms die (**ammonification**).

chapter: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life
prompt: Match each bacterium with its job in the nitrogen cycle.

image.alt: Nitrogen moving between the air, a pea plant and the soil

right.text: Converts ammonia into nitrite
Converts nitrate back into nitrogen gas
Fixes N₂ into ammonia inside legume root nodules
Converts nitrite into nitrate
Fixes N₂ into ammonia while living freely in the soil

hint: Nitroso- comes before Nitro- in the chain: ammonia → nitrite → nitrate.
explanation: **Nitrogen fixation**: *Rhizobium* (in root nodules) and *Azotobacter* (free in the soil) turn N₂ into ammonia. **Nitrification**: *Nitrosomonas* turns ammonia into nitrite ($\text{NO}_2^-$) and *Nitrobacter* turns nitrite into nitrate ($\text{NO}_3^-$). **Denitrification**: *Pseudomonas* turns some nitrate back into N₂ gas, completing the cycle.

prompt: Follow a nitrogen atom from the air into a plant and back into the soil. Arrange the steps in order.

image.alt: Nitrogen moving between the air, a pea plant and the soil

items.text: Nitrite is converted into nitrate
Bacteria fix N₂ from the air into ammonia
The plant dies and decomposers return ammonia to the soil
Ammonia is converted into nitrite
The plant absorbs nitrate and builds proteins

hint: Plants cannot use N₂ directly; it must be changed in steps first.
explanation: N₂ is unreactive, so it is first **fixed** into ammonia. **Nitrification** turns ammonia into nitrite and then nitrate. Plants **assimilate** nitrate to make proteins and nucleic acids, and animals get nitrogen by eating plants. When organisms die, decomposers carry out **ammonification**, returning ammonia to the soil, while denitrifying bacteria send some nitrate back to the air.

prompt: Which of these processes **use up oxygen** from the atmosphere? Select all that apply.

image.alt: A plant, a person, a campfire and a rusting bucket under the open sky

options.text: Respiration by plants and animals
Photosynthesis
Combustion of fuels
Formation of oxides, such as rusting
Transpiration from leaves
Nitrogen fixation by *Rhizobium*

hint: Only one process on the list puts oxygen back.
explanation: Atmospheric oxygen (about 21% of air) is used in **respiration**, **combustion** and **oxide formation** (such as rusting), and these processes release CO₂ or lock oxygen into compounds. **Photosynthesis** restores it, using sunlight, water and CO₂ to make glucose and release O₂. Transpiration releases water vapour, and nitrogen fixation does not use oxygen from the air.

prompt: Arrange the steps of **eutrophication** in the order they happen.

image.alt: A farm on a slope draining into a lake covered with green scum

items.text: Algae grow rapidly and cover the water (algal bloom)
Farmers put too much fertiliser on their fields
Fish die and the fishery is harmed
Rain washes excess nitrates into the lake
Oxygen in the water gets used up

hint: The nutrients must reach the water before the algae can use them.
explanation: Overuse of **fertilisers** adds excess nitrogen; rain carries **nitrates** into rivers and lakes; algae multiply into an **algal bloom**; the bloom **depletes oxygen**; and **fish die**. This is **eutrophication**, a human disruption of the nitrogen cycle that threatens water bodies and coastal fisheries.

chapter: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life
prompt: A large forest is cleared. Which of these are likely effects? Select all that apply.

image.alt: A green forest beside a cleared hillside with stumps and muddy water

options.text: Less photosynthesis, so less CO₂ is removed from the air
Less transpiration, which can reduce local rainfall
More soil erosion, because no roots hold the soil
A change in the albedo of the land surface
More groundwater recharge, because rain no longer falls on leaves
Greater biodiversity, because open land makes new habitats

hint: Trees affect air, water, soil and living things all at once.
explanation: Clearing forests means **less photosynthesis** (so less CO₂ removed and less O₂ released) and **less transpiration**, which can lower local rainfall. It **alters surface albedo**, and without roots **soil erosion** rises, so rivers carry more mud. Over time habitats are destroyed and **biodiversity declines**. Bare, eroding soil sheds rain as run-off instead of letting it soak in, so groundwater recharge does not improve.
